To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the shot noise of a capacitively coupled double quantum dot can be positive in an asymmetric setup.
positive shot noise correlations can arise in asymmetrically coupled double quantum dots.
positive correlations in the current are observed in a system of two coupled quantum dots.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how to control and manipulate the temporal correlations of the tunneling current.
the shot noise behavior in a system of two quantum dots coupled by the Coulomb interaction.
the question how the shot noise properties of quantum systems can be controlled by external parameters and how the noise can be used as a diagnostic tool.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sign of the current-current correlations can change from negative to positive with decreasing bias voltage.
the sign of the correlations depends on the asymmetry in tunneling rates and the coupling strength of the dots.
the bunching of electrons can be attributed to the Coulomb interaction of the quantum dot states.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
positive correlations in the shot noise of tunneling through coupled quantum dots are possible in asymmetric setups, but only for a limited parameter range.
in an asymmetric setup the shot noise can be enhanced or suppressed by varying the tunneling rates of the quantum dots.
the bunching effect is not restricted to the case of two identical quantum dot states, but can also appear in the case of two different quantum dots.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bunching of electrons in the tunneling events can be controlled by tuning the asymmetry of the system and the applied gate voltages.
a simple Master equation description of tunneling processes is sufficient to capture the essential features of the shot noise behavior.
a negative correlation in the tunneling of electrons from one dot to the other can be compensated by positive correlations between the tunneling events of the individual dots.
